# The Hateful Immortals: A Documentary History of the Greenbriar-Chen Marriage (1847–2024)

*Dr. Amelia Thornton, Department of Parahuman Studies, Columbia University*
*Journal of Extraordinary Biographical Research, Vol. 41, No. 2 (2024)*

---

## I. Preliminary Remarks

It is necessary to establish certain facts before any account of this kind can proceed in good faith.

First: that in the world as it has existed since at least the fifteenth century, and almost certainly longer, a minority of human beings—estimated between 4 and 7 percent of the global population, depending on methodology and era—manifest anomalous abilities at or around the onset of puberty. These abilities range from the trivial (chromatophoric skin changes, minor thermal regulation) to the extraordinary (flight, molecular restructuring, temporal displacement). No predictive model has successfully determined which individuals will manifest, nor what form their abilities will take. They arrive as weather arrives: without consent, without explanation, and with consequences that must simply be lived through.

Second: that among the many thousands of documented cases in the modern archive, precisely two concern us here.

Third: that the marriage of Margaret Greenbriar and James Chen, solemnized in Boston on the fourteenth of June, 1851, and persisting—without annulment, divorce, or dissolution of any recognized legal form—to the date of this writing, constitutes the longest-documented case of mutual domestic entrapment in human history. I use the word *entrapment* with deliberation and with full awareness that both subjects would contest it, though they would contest it for opposite reasons.

My primary sources across what follows include: the municipal and parish records of Boston, Massachusetts (1847–1878); the immigration and customs files of France, Argentina, Brazil, Japan, Portugal, New Zealand, and South Africa; six volumes of court transcripts spanning four continents; three separate asylum intake assessments (two for Margaret, one for James); property deeds in eleven countries; a 1923 monograph on "Persistent Cognitive Hyper-Retention" that describes its subject as "Patient M.G." with a transparency that would have been comical had the intervening century not rendered it moot; 247 letters and fragments of letters, of which approximately sixty are in Margaret's hand and the remainder in the hands of acquaintances, attorneys, landlords, physicians, and, in one case, a Buenos Aires ethnomusicologist who had no idea what he was recording; and a single surviving daguerreotype, dated June 1851, which I will describe presently.

I should note that I requested interviews with both subjects. Margaret Greenbriar-Chen agreed immediately and with a graciousness that I found, I confess, somewhat unsettling—as though she had been waiting for the question for a very long time and was relieved that someone had finally thought to ask it in the right institutional register. James Chen declined. His response, relayed through Margaret, was: "What's one more person who thinks they understand?"

I present this remark without commentary. The reader will have the whole of what follows in which to decide whether it reflects wisdom, exhaustion, or the particular cruelty of a man who has survived everything except the desire to be known.

---

## II. The Daguerreotype — Boston, 1847–1851

Margaret Greenbriar's ability manifested on the eleventh of March, 1847, during a Latin recitation at the Mount Vernon Female Seminary. She was nineteen years old. She had been asked to decline the verb *meminisse*—"to remember," defective, existing only in the perfect tense, a fact whose irony she would not appreciate for several decades—and as she opened her mouth to speak, something shifted. She has described the sensation in three separate recorded accounts, each given decades apart, and each identical to the word, to the pause, to the breath:

> It was as though a door opened in a room I had not known was closed. And behind the door was everything. Every word I had ever read, heard, spoken, or overheard. Every face. Every meal. Every quality of light through every window I had ever sat beside. All of it, not as memory is—dim, partial, fondly or fearfully distorted—but as it *was*. As it *is*. Present tense. Undiminished. I could hear my mother singing in the kitchen when I was four. I could feel the grain of the bannister under my hand at age eleven. I could smell the13th of October, 1839. I did not yet understand that this door, once opened, does not close.

The seminary records note that she completed the recitation flawlessly and then sat down and wept for forty minutes.

James Chen's manifestation was, by contrast, blunt. He was twenty-one, employed at his father's warehouse on the wharves—his father being Chen Wei-Lin, a Cantonese merchant of moderate success who had married one Bridget Flanagan of County Cork in a union that had scandalized precisely the communities one would expect and delighted precisely no one. James was on the second floor of the warehouse when three structural beams gave way simultaneously. The building came down on top of him. Two men were killed. James walked out of the rubble without a cut, a bruise, or a speck of dust in his lungs.

The *Boston Courier* reported the collapse. It did not mention James's survival specifically, but a letter from Bridget Chen to her sister in Ireland—one of only four documents in the family's hand to survive—notes, with what one reads as either maternal pride or maternal dread: "Jamie came through without so much as a torn shirt. The doctors say it is a Power. His father has not spoken since."

They met, as many "specials" of the era met, at the edges—the margins of polite society where the anomalous were herded with a mixture of fascination and disgust. Boston in the late 1840s maintained no formal registry of parahuman individuals, but the social architecture accomplished what bureaucracy had not yet attempted: powered persons found themselves excluded from certain churches, certain clubs, certain dinner tables, and thus gravitationally drawn to each other's company. A small circle formed around the salon of Mrs. Adelaide Proctor, herself a telepath of limited range, who hosted Thursday evenings for what she called, with magnificent delusion, "the Gifted of the Commonwealth."

I have found no direct account of James and Margaret's first meeting. There are fragments: a letter from Margaret to a school friend, dated April 1850, in which she mentions "a young man of mixed parentage and considerable stubbornness who has taken to arguing with me about Emerson"; a bill of sale showing James purchased a volume of Tennyson from a Cornhill bookseller, which, given that no other evidence suggests James had any interest in poetry before or since, may constitute a courtship document. There is a gap here that even Margaret's perfect memory cannot fill for the outside observer—she possesses the complete internal record, every glance and inflection, but what she shared with me in our interviews was selective and, I believe, deliberately so. She remembers everything. She does not owe us everything.

What survives publicly is the daguerreotype.

It measures three and a quarter by four and a quarter inches. The case is leather, water-damaged, held together with a strip of linen that appears to have been torn from a bedsheet. Inside, the silver plate shows two figures in wedding clothes standing before a painted backdrop of improbable Grecian columns. Margaret wears a dark dress—white wedding gowns were fashionable but not universal—with a high collar and sleeves to the wrist. James wears a suit that fits poorly across the shoulders, suggesting it was borrowed. They are not looking at the camera.

They are looking at each other.

Margaret's right hand grips James's left forearm. Even accounting for the long exposure time, which required absolute stillness and which renders most daguerreotype subjects into waxwork rigidity, the pressure of her grip is visible. The knuckles are white. She is holding on to him with a force that, depending on one's interpretation, communicates either that she has found the thing she will not release or that she already knows she will need to hold this tightly, for this long, and has started early.

Their expressions are difficult to read. The chemistry of the daguerreotype, and the seventeen decades since, have introduced a haze at precisely the region of the eyes. What remains is the architecture of two faces turned toward each other with an intensity the medium cannot quite resolve. Rapture or terror—the photographic technology of the era cannot distinguish.

I have spent more time with this image than professional decorum can justify. It is, I remind myself, a piece of treated silver. It is not the marriage. It is the residue of a single afternoon in June when two young people who did not yet know what they were stood still long enough for the light to fix them.

Margaret, when I showed her a high-resolution scan during our interview, looked at it for a long time and then said: "His tie was crooked. You can't see it in the reproduction, but it was. I fixed it twice and it wouldn't stay. I remember the thread count of the silk."

She paused.

"I remember everything about that day. I wish that were an exaggeration."

---

## III. The First Wound That Never Heals — 1852

In the literature of parahuman domestic studies—a field that barely existed before this case compelled its creation—there is a concept borrowed from materials science: the *stress riser*. In metallurgy, a stress riser is a point of concentrated strain, often microscopic, often invisible, from which a fracture propagates. A hairline flaw in a steel beam. A nick in a turbine blade. It is not the point of failure; it is the point from which failure becomes, given sufficient time and pressure, inevitable.

The Greenbriar-Chen marriage's first documented stress riser is an event I have termed the Incident of the Dropped Tureen.

The primary source is Margaret's own account, given in 1993 to Dr. Paulo Ferreira of the University of São Paulo, who was conducting a longitudinal study of parahuman cognitive function and who did not, at the time, realize that his subject was also the subject of four outstanding warrants for identity fraud across two continents. Margaret's account, transcribed from a recorded interview, is characteristically total:

> It was the evening of November the fourteenth, 1852. A Tuesday. The temperature was forty-one degrees Fahrenheit; I know because I had checked the thermometer on the back porch at half past four and the mercury was at forty-one and one-quarter, and by the time James came home it had not changed. I was making a fish chowder. Haddock. The recipe was my mother's—she used salt pork where most used bacon, and I have never changed this. James had gone to purchase lamp oil from a shop on Tremont Street, and he came back in a state I recognized: the jaw set, the shoulders drawn up, the way he breathed through his nose rather than his mouth when he was preventing himself from shouting in public and had not yet released the shout.
>
> He told me that the shopkeeper—a Mr. Phelps, whose establishment was at the corner of Tremont and Winter, and whose left eyelid had a tic when he was uncomfortable—had refused to serve him. Had pretended not to see him at the counter. Had served two other men who came in after him. When James spoke, Mr. Phelps startled and said he hadn't noticed him, which was a lie of the kind that requires the liar to believe you are not worth the effort of a better one.
>
> I made the mistake of responding. I do not remember what I said—no, that is not true. I remember precisely what I said. I said: "Perhaps if you spoke to him more gently." I knew as I said it that it was wrong, that it was the wrong thing, that I was siding with the geometry of the room rather than with him. But I said it. I have often thought about why. I believe I was afraid, though not of James. I was afraid of the scope of the injustice, which was so large and so daily and so durably woven into the world that I could not look at it directly without feeling that it would swallow both of us, and so I made it small. I made it a matter of tone. I have never forgiven myself for this, though James has, many times, because James forgives everything, which is its own kind of cruelty when you are married to someone who forgives nothing, least of all herself.
>
> He said—and I will give you the words as he said them, because I have no choice, because they exist in me with the same fidelity as the sound of my own breathing—he said: "You sound exactly like your mother. The same simpering instinct to make everything my fault and call it concern."
>
> The pitch of his voice was a D-flat below middle C. He was standing four feet from me. The coal smoke on his jacket was from the anthracite they burned at the shop, which has a different smell from the bituminous we used at home—sharper, more metallic. The room was fifty-eight degrees. The tureen was in my hands—the white one with the blue chrysanthemum pattern, which had a chip on the left handle from when I had knocked it against the basin the previous March—and when he said "simpering" I felt my hands open. Not as a decision. As a consequence.
>
> The tureen hit the floor and broke into five pieces. I can draw you a map of the fragments. The chowder spread in an oblong pattern toward the stove. The silence afterward lasted eleven seconds. I counted them then and I have counted them since and they have never become fewer.

The corroborating account is thinner—necessarily so. James Chen addressed the evening of November 14, 1852, in a deposition given in 1911 in connection with an unrelated property dispute in Marseilles, in which opposing counsel, having somehow obtained records linking James to his earlier Boston identity, attempted to establish a pattern of domestic instability. James's response, as recorded by the court stenographer, was:

> I do not recall the specific evening. I am sure I was unkind on many occasions. I was a young man with a young man's cruelties. If you are asking whether I struck my wife, I did not. If you are asking whether I wounded her, I am certain I did. I do not remember with what words. That is not evasion. It is the ordinary condition of being a person who has lived long enough for the ordinary to accumulate beyond retrieval.

"I do not remember." Not denial. Not deflection. The ordinary human mercy of forgetting—the neural kindness that softens edges, compresses decades, allows a Tuesday in 1852 to dissolve into the general sediment of a long life. Every person who has been married for even ten years knows this mercy: the gift of not being able to reproduce the exact words of the worst thing you ever said at dinner on a November night.

Margaret's power has revoked this mercy. For her, the tureen is always falling. James is always standing four feet away, smelling of anthracite, his voice pitched at D-flat. The silence is always eleven seconds long and has never, in 172 years, resolved into the twelfth.

I want to be precise about something. James was not wrong to be angry. He had been humiliated by a shopkeeper in a city that had humiliated him daily since birth—for his father's country, for his mother's poverty, for the shape of his face, for the Power that marked him as both useful and dangerous. Margaret was not wrong to be afraid. She was twenty-four years old and the scope of what her husband faced was something she could perceive but not solve and could not, in 1852, even adequately name, because the vocabulary of structural oppression had not yet been assembled, and what she had instead was a fish chowder and a simpering instinct toward peace that she already hated in herself.

They were both twenty-something and unkind and cornered and did not yet know that they would have to live with this evening forever—him in the abstract, her in high fidelity.

The house in which the tureen fell stood at 14 Myrtle Street, Boston. It was demolished in 1903 to make way for a rooming house that was itself demolished in 1952. The lot is now a parking garage.

The tureen is still falling.
